title: How the web works
summary: A page starts as a request and becomes something a browser can display.
points: A browser is a client. A server responds with resources such as an HTML document; a page may request several more files.
DNS helps resolve a domain name to an IP address. A URL also describes the scheme and the path of a resource.
HTML gives content structure, CSS controls presentation, and JavaScript adds programmable behavior.
HTTP responses have status codes: 200 means success, 404 means the requested resource was not found, and 500 indicates a server error.
HTTPS protects data in transit using TLS. It does not prove that the content of a site is trustworthy.
output: The browser requests /study/week-1.html from example.com using HTTPS. The fragment in a URL such as #tasks is handled by the browser and is not sent in the HTTP request.
mistake: A domain is not a complete website, and opening a file on your own computer does not publish it.
challenge: Open browser developer tools, select Network, then reload a public page. Find the document request, its status, and one image request.

diagram.title: How the web works
diagram.caption: The browser requests a resource; the response supplies data to render.

title: Editor & first page
summary: Keep a small, understandable project folder and learn the edit–save–refresh loop.
points: Use a plain-text code editor. Save your entry page as index.html, not index.html.txt.
Create an images folder for assets. Use consistent lowercase file names and match spelling and case in links.
Open the HTML file in a browser. A local development server is useful later when features need HTTP; a basic static page also opens as a file.
Save in the editor before refreshing the browser. Developer-tools edits are usually temporary and do not update your source file.
Terminal commands run relative to your current directory. pwd shows it; ls lists entries; cd changes directory. Windows command syntax can differ.
code:
My study week

One small step today.
output: The browser tab says My planner. The page shows a main heading and a paragraph. Edit the paragraph, save, and refresh to see your change.
mistake: A rich-text document is not an HTML source file. Check file extensions when the browser displays the source instead of rendering it.
challenge: Create a planner folder, save index.html, and change its paragraph twice. Explain which copy is saved on disk and which is displayed in the browser.

diagram.title: Editor & first page
diagram.caption: A saved source file is your durable copy; refresh loads its latest contents.

title: Git & GitHub basics
summary: Keep meaningful snapshots locally, then share them through a remote repository.
points: Git is version-control software. GitHub hosts repositories and collaboration tools; a local Git repository works without GitHub.
git status shows what changed. git diff shows unstaged changes; git diff --staged shows the next proposed snapshot.
git add stages chosen changes. git commit records the staged snapshot locally; git push sends commits to a configured remote.
Create a branch for a focused change. A pull request is a review workflow, not the same operation as creating a commit.
Never commit passwords, tokens, or private configuration. A .gitignore rule does not remove a secret that is already tracked or erase its history.

rows: Create and switch to a branch

code:
# Run inside your own new planner folder
git init
git status
git add index.html
git diff --staged
git commit -m "Add planner page"
git switch -c add-schedule
output: After configuring your Git author name/email if requested, the commit records index.html locally. Creating the branch does not publish anything; connecting a remote and pushing is a separate step.
mistake: Saving a file, staging it, committing it, and pushing it are four different actions.
challenge: Initialize your practice folder, commit the first page, create add-schedule, and commit a heading change. Use git log --oneline to inspect the two snapshots. Publish only your practice files to your own repository.

diagram.title: Git & GitHub basics
diagram.caption: Inspect what you stage before you create a snapshot. Push is a separate remote action.

title: HTML document structure
summary: Separate page metadata from the content people read.
points: <!doctype html> selects standards mode. The html element wraps the document; lang identifies its language.
The head holds metadata such as title, character encoding, and viewport settings. The body contains page content.
Elements often have opening and closing tags. Nest them in reverse order: the last element opened is the first one closed.
Attributes add information to an opening tag. Quote attribute values; keep each id unique within its document.
Void elements such as img, input, and meta have no closing tag. Use < when you want a literal less-than character in text.
code:
Study planner

Read <main> as text.
output: The tab title and visible h1 both say Study planner, but they are separate elements. The paragraph displays <main> as text rather than creating an element.
mistake: Browser error recovery can hide invalid nesting. A page looking plausible does not prove its HTML is valid.
challenge: Add a useful title, language, UTF-8 declaration, and viewport to your planner. Introduce one misnested tag, inspect the DOM, then fix the source.

diagram.title: HTML document structure
diagram.caption: Metadata and content have different jobs inside one document.

title: Text & lists
summary: Use structure to make a page easy to scan and navigate.
points: Use a descriptive h1 for the page’s main heading, then h2 and h3 for nested sections. Choose heading ranks by structure, not visual size.
p marks a paragraph. Ordinary whitespace is collapsed when rendered; repeated spaces are not a layout tool.
ul is an unordered list, ol is an ordered list, and li is a list item. Use an ordered list when sequence matters.
strong expresses importance and em expresses stress emphasis. Styling alone does not communicate the same meaning.
Use code for code text and pre when preserving spaces and line breaks matters. Escape markup inside code examples.
code:
Study planner

Today’s steps

  1. Read one lesson.
  2. Build a small example.

Remember: save your work.
output: The list is numbered because the order matters. Remember has importance; the main title and the section heading have different ranks.
mistake: Adding empty paragraphs or many br elements to create spacing makes the structure confusing. Layout belongs in CSS.
challenge: Write a course overview with a page heading, two section headings, a three-step ordered list, and an unordered list of supplies.

diagram.title: Text & lists
diagram.caption: A clear hierarchy helps both scanning and assistive navigation.

title: Links & paths
summary: Connect pages with destinations that remain meaningful when your project moves.
points: An a element with href creates a hyperlink. Link text should explain the destination rather than saying only “click here”.
A relative path resolves from the current document’s location. ../ moves up one folder; a leading / starts at the website origin’s root.
An absolute HTTPS URL includes its origin. A fragment such as #tasks targets an element with id="tasks" on the page.
A file path on your computer is not a public URL. Test links from nested pages and on a case-sensitive host.
Use a link for navigation and a button for an action. If a new tab is necessary, make it clear; rel="noopener" explicitly separates opener access.
code:
Home Study schedule Today’s tasks

Today’s tasks
output: The first two links navigate to files in the current folder. The third moves to the tasks section in this document.
mistake: href="#" is not a substitute for a working destination. It can unexpectedly move the page to the top.
challenge: Create schedule.html and link both pages to each other. Move schedule.html into a pages folder, update both relative links, and test again.

diagram.title: Links & paths
diagram.caption: A useful link explains both where it goes and how to get there.

title: Images & media
summary: Include meaningful alternatives so visual and audio content can be understood in different ways.
points: img uses src for the image URL and alt for its text alternative. Describe the image’s purpose in this context, not every pixel.
Use alt="" for a purely decorative image. Omitting alt is different from deliberately supplying an empty alternative.
width and height help reserve the image’s layout space. Use appropriately sized files; loading="lazy" suits off-screen images rather than the main above-the-fold image.
figure can group an image with figcaption. A caption is visible context and does not automatically replace alt.
audio and video can expose native controls. Provide appropriate captions/transcripts and avoid forcing autoplay. A track element can reference a WebVTT caption file.
output: When week.png exists at that path, the image has a visible caption and a separate text alternative. If the file is missing, the alternative still communicates its purpose.
mistake: A file name like photo7.png is usually not a useful text alternative. Captions and alternative text serve different needs.
challenge: Add one meaningful image and one decorative image to your planner. Write a suitable alternative for each, then inspect the page with images unavailable.

diagram.title: Images & media
diagram.caption: Make the meaning available even when the media cannot be perceived.

title: Semantic page layout
summary: Choose elements for the meaning of the content they contain.
points: header introduces a page or section. nav identifies major navigation; footer contains closing or related information.
main identifies the dominant content. Keep one visible main area on a typical page.
article is suitable for self-contained content. section groups a thematic part, normally with a heading; aside holds tangential content.
div and span are generic containers. Use them when no more meaningful element fits, not as replacements for every element.
A skip link to the main content lets keyboard users bypass repeated navigation. Keep the reading order logical before adding CSS.
code:
Skip to content

Study planner

Home

This week

Start with HTML.

Made for learning.
output: The page exposes meaningful regions. The skip link points past the navigation to the main content.
mistake: A section is not just a convenient styling box. If it has no thematic meaning, a div may be more appropriate.
challenge: Restructure your planner with header, nav, main, and footer. Add a skip link and verify its destination using the keyboard.

diagram.title: Semantic page layout
diagram.caption: Semantic regions explain the page without relying on its visual layout.

title: Accessible data tables
summary: Use tables for relationships between rows and columns, not for page layout.
points: table contains tabular data. A caption names the table; tr creates a row, th a header cell, and td a data cell.
Use scope="col" for simple column headers and scope="row" for row headers. Complex tables need more careful associations.
thead and tbody group header rows and data rows. These groups do not replace the need for actual header cells.
Keep tables simple and readable on small screens. Do not merge cells unnecessarily or rely on color alone.
Use CSS layout tools for positioning a page. Reserve tables for data such as a study schedule.
output: The caption names the schedule. Day and Topic are column headers; Monday and Tuesday are row headers.
mistake: Bold text inside td is still a data cell. Use th to communicate the header relationship.
challenge: Create a three-day schedule with a caption, column headings, and day names as row headings. Read a cell and identify its two headers.

diagram.title: Accessible data tables
diagram.caption: A cell is easier to understand when its table and headers are clear.

title: Forms & validation
summary: Name each control, explain what is required, and understand where submission goes.
points: Connect a visible label’s for attribute to the control’s id. name determines the field key used during submission.
Choose an appropriate input type such as email, date, or checkbox. Use textarea for multi-line text and select for a list of options.
Group related choices with fieldset and legend. Radio buttons in the same named group allow one selection; checkboxes allow independent selections.
required and other constraints provide browser validation. This improves feedback but does not replace server validation or authorization.
form action is the destination; method controls the submission method. GET puts submitted data in the query string; POST sends a request body. HTTPS is still needed.
Give buttons explicit types. type="button" performs no form submission by itself; type="submit" submits a form.

rows: Connect a label to a control

code:
<form action="/tasks" method="post">
  <label for="task">Task title</label>
  <input id="task" name="title" required>
  <label for="due">Due date</label>
  <input id="due" name="due" type="date">
  <button type="submit">Save task</button>
</form>
output: The browser checks required fields before a normal submission. A real /tasks server endpoint must receive and validate the request; this snippet alone does not store a task.
mistake: A placeholder disappears during entry and is not a replacement for a visible label. A POST request is not automatically encrypted.
challenge: Add a labelled task-entry form with a required title and a date field. Test an empty title. Keep the local prototype honest: saving needs behavior or a backend added in a later phase.

diagram.title: Forms & validation
diagram.caption: Explain the field, accept input, and validate again on the server.

title: Accessibility & debugging
summary: Test whether people can understand and operate the page, not just whether it looks right.
points: Navigate with Tab and Shift+Tab. Native links and buttons support keyboard interaction; do not replace them with clickable div elements.
Keep a visible focus indicator and a logical source order. Avoid positive tabindex values that create a surprising navigation order.
Inspect headings, landmarks, control names, and image alternatives. Prefer native HTML semantics before adding ARIA.
Use developer tools to inspect the DOM and failed network requests. Browser-repaired markup can differ from your source.
Validate markup, but also perform manual keyboard and zoom checks. Automated tools cannot establish complete accessibility.
aria-label supplies an accessible name when appropriate. It does not turn an otherwise inert element into a functioning button.

rows: Can I reach and operate controls?

code:
Skip to content

Study tasks

This static prototype has no task-saving behavior yet.
output: The native button can receive keyboard focus. It does not add a task until behavior is implemented; clear prototype copy prevents a false expectation.
mistake: An ARIA role does not implement keyboard events. An HTML validator passing does not prove the whole experience is accessible.
challenge: Check your planner with only the keyboard, at 200% zoom, and with a narrow viewport. Fix at least one issue and explain why the change helps.

diagram.title: Accessibility & debugging
diagram.caption: Combine markup checks with real interaction checks.

title: Build a student planner
summary: Combine the course into a small website that you can explain and extend.
points: Create index.html, schedule.html, and tasks.html with descriptive titles, a language, a main heading, and shared navigation.
Use semantic regions on each page, real relative links, a captioned schedule table, and visibly labelled task controls.
Keep this version static. Do not claim tasks are saved or accounts are protected before those capabilities exist.
Use small Git commits to record meaningful milestones: structure, schedule, forms, and fixes. Add a README explaining how to open the pages.
Self-review: follow every link in both directions, test keyboard navigation and image alternatives, check nesting, and inspect at narrow widths.
Explain one design decision aloud. Your MCQ score checks recall; a working project and your explanation demonstrate different skills.

rows: Explain the planner and link its pages
Collect inputs with honest prototype limits

code:
planner/
  index.html
  schedule.html
  tasks.html
  images/
  README.md

# Suggested milestones
# 1. Add semantic page structure
# 2. Connect the schedule and task pages
# 3. Review labels, links, and keyboard navigation
output: Completion means your three pages work together and pass your self-review. The supplied starter is one page; split and extend it yourself. CSS, interaction, storage, accounts, and deployment come later.
mistake: Copying a finished page without explaining its structure hides gaps. Start from the brief and use the starter only when helpful.
challenge: Finish the three pages. In your README, describe two decisions, one issue you fixed, and one limitation left for the next course. Self-check the brief before marking this topic complete.

diagram.title: Build a student planner
diagram.caption: A small, honest project is a foundation you can keep improving.
